title: Insights for strengthening wildlife trade regulations: Evidence from local stakeholders and regulatory officials in Nigeria
content:
Since illegal wildlife trade remains a major threat to vultures across most African countries, and country-level regulations alone are not enough to stop it, our study shows that local communities, traditional medicine practitioners, traders and government agencies all have valuable knowledge that can improve wildlife protection when they work together. We demonstrated that involving local stakeholders in identifying species that need legal protection enables governments to make better decisions, strengthen law enforcement and respond more effectively to changing trade patterns. Collectively, our findings suggest that protecting endangered species requires not only stronger laws but also community participation, better information sharing, continuous learning and collaboration to build a more effective and sustainable conservation system.


Abstract

The Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species of Wild Fauna and Flora (CITES), a globally recognised wildlife trade treaty, has shaped wildlife trade policy. However, whether the implementation of the global wildlife trade treaty through an act of the National Assembly in Nigeria has incorporated the diverse institutional and local knowledge systems remains unexplored. Here, we conducted purposive interviews comprising 50 local stakeholders and 50 wildlife trade regulators to assess the impact of wildlife regulations on the trade of endangered African vulture species in Nigeria. We found few documented interventions and weakening institutional capacity of regulatory agencies to curb vulture trade effectively, as a result of limited training, inconsistent enforcement and uneven implementation of the Nigerian wildlife trade regulations across local communities. Furthermore, we found that the level of awareness was low among the many interviewed officials of state-established regulatory agencies. Policy implication. Collectively, our findings underscore the need for Nigerian wildlife regulatory agencies at the country level to establish a systematic and collaborative process for strengthening domestic wildlife laws and agencies through training, awareness and stakeholder engagement.
